paragraphs: The strongest man is never strong enough to remain master forever, unless he turns strength into right and obedience into duty. From this comes the right of the strongest. It seems to be meant ironically, yet it is actually laid down as a fundamental principle. Are we never to be given an explanation of the phrase? Force is a physical power, and I do not see what moral effect it can have. Yielding to force is an act of necessity, not of will; at most it is an act of prudence. In what sense could it be a duty?

Suppose for a moment that this so-called “right” exists. I maintain that the only outcome is a heap of inexplicable nonsense. If force creates right, the effect changes whenever the cause does: any force greater than the first inherits its right. Once it is possible to disobey without being punished, disobedience is legitimate. And since the strongest is always in the right, the only thing that matters is to act so as to become the strongest. But what sort of right perishes when force gives out? If we must obey because we are forced, there is no need to obey because we ought; and if we are not forced to obey, we have no obligation to do so. Plainly, the word “right” adds nothing to force. Here it means nothing whatever.

Obey the powers that be. If this means yield to force, it is a good precept but unnecessary: I can guarantee that it will never be violated. All power comes from God, I admit; but so does all sickness. Does that mean we are forbidden to call the doctor? A brigand surprises me at the edge of a wood. Must I not only hand over my purse under compulsion, but, even if I could keep it back, am I in conscience bound to give it up? For certainly the pistol he holds is also a power.
Let us then grant that force does not create right, and that we are obliged to obey only legitimate powers. In that case, my original question returns.
